# Antenna Mounts for Tower Structures

{% hint style="warning" %}
Please note: This guide is still in its draft stages. Some of the information presented here may be inaccurate or imcomplete.
{% endhint %}

Mounting Antennas on pre-existing tower structures may seem complex, but can be simplified in very easy and intuitive ways. The amount of variation possible is limited only by one's imagination, but typically the simplest solution can be the most robust and most reliable long term solution. &#x20;

For mounting on Tower-like structures, you are limited to 3 options:  &#x20;

[A.) Mounting to the top mast of a tower](antenna-mounts-for-tower-structures.md#option-a-mounting-to-the-top-mast-of-a-tower)&#x20;

[B.) Mounting to a singular leg ](antenna-mounts-for-tower-structures.md#option-b-mounting-to-a-singular-leg)

[C.) Mounting to the 'face' of the tower via 2 legs](antenna-mounts-for-tower-structures.md#option-c-mounting-to-the-face-of-the-tower-via-2-legs)

### Option A: Mounting to the top mast of a tower

This is the simplest, but is often the first to be eliminated for pre-existing towers as the top mast is either already full or simply does not exist as a feature of the tower. Ideally coaxial runs for Motus setups should not exceed 60ft to minimize signal loss (see antenna diagrams), and existing structures often exceed this threshold.&#x20;

### Option B: Mounting to a singular leg

This can be as simple as connecting the antenna directly to the leg of the tower, though this should only ever be a temporary / short term measure as it is always best to have separation from the tower for proper signal transfer, and to avoid encroaching on tower access via climbing. Large towers often have a designated 'climbing face' with a built in ladder and climbing arrest system, and space needs to be free of any/all obstructions. The utilization of extended mounts is often the best approach, but gravity and overall wind resistance are the limiting factors as the mount only has two contact points. These mounts are best used on larger structures where the legs are capable of withstanding the torsion forces applied by wind loading. <br>

### Option C: Mounting to the 'face' of the tower via 2 legs

This mount offers the best support, and is the method of choice for most applications. This mount consists of two lengths of aluminum angle that attach horizontally to the 'face' of the tower. One or two vertical mast(s) are attached to the end(s) of the angle. When installing antennas with heavier wind loads (e.g., 9-element 166 yagis), mount each antenna on its own dedicated mast to reduce stress on the tower.&#x20;

#### Attaching to Tubular legs vs Formed Channel Legs

Lattice towers can be made from tubular legs or formed channel legs. UBolts are used to attach aluminum angle to tubular legs. To attach to formed channel legs, you need to use galvanized hex bolts through the flat face (middle) of the formed channel legs of the tower. Use existing holes when possible. Only drill new holes (with steel drill bits) if necessary and with station owner permissions as it can compromise the integrity of the structure. Avoid drilling near existing bolts or joints.

#### Attaching one vs two vertical masts

In all cases, two lengths of aluminum angle (1/4" x 2-1/2" x 2-1/2" x 10 ft) are used to attach horizontally to the 'face' of the tower, utilizing u-bolts or hex bolts (see [above](antenna-mounts-for-tower-structures.md#attaching-to-tubular-legs-vs-formed-channel-legs)) at each leg. One or two vertical mast(s) (1.5 inch / 16 gauge / 5 foot) are attached to the end(s) of the angle.&#x20;

When custom making a face mount, it is important to keep in mind that for free standing towers, there is always a taper. This comes into play when designing the mounts, as you must be careful to mount the pipe as close to vertical as possible. The easiest way to ensure that the pipe will be mounted vertically, is by measuring out from your center, or plumb line on your mounts. The mounts shown here are approximately 26" apart, which for this tower amounted to a difference of ¾" between the two measurements. In order to properly place the vertical mounting pipe, I first measured between both inner u-bolt holes to find the exact center of the mount on the tower face. Once you have your center line (marked as a 'C' with a line through it) you simply measure the same distance from the center for each mount to were the pipe will be attached. For smaller mounts a single u bolt at each connection point is sufficient, but for larger mounts or for heavier loads (including longer yagis resulting in larger wind loads) double u bolts should be a consideration.&#x20;

When installing heavier wind load antennas such as 9-element 166 yagis, mount each antenna on its own dedicated mast to reduce stress on the tower. Begin by attaching two horizontal cross arms made from aluminum angle (1/4" x 2-1/2" x 2-1/2" x 10 ft) to the face of the tower, bolting through both legs of the angle. At the outer ends of these cross arms, install secondary vertical masts (1.5 inch diameter, 16-gauge, 5 ft long), ensuring there is enough clearance between the tower leg and each mast to allow the antennas to be oriented freely without their elements contacting the tower structure (see table above).&#x20;

Select mounting points on the tower for the aluminum angle, using existing holes wherever possible. If new holes must be drilled, use steel drill bits and avoid placing holes near existing bolts or joints. Drill through the flat face (center) of the tower\`s formed channel legs, starting with a small pilot hole and gradually increasing to the required diameter to accommodate the bolt shank. Repeat this process on both tower legs, ensuring that corresponding holes are perfectly level and aligned horizontally. Leave approximately 2 ft of vertical spacing between the upper and lower aluminum angle, and duplicate the same hole pattern for both levels.  &#x20;

Measure the center-to-center distance between holes across the two legs for both the top and bottom sets, noting that the distances may differ slightly if the tower tapers (as discussed above). Use these measurements to locate the exact center (plumb line) of the tower face by measuring between the bolt holes. Transfer this centerline to the aluminum angle by marking its midpoint, then measure outward from the center to match the bolt hole positions on each tower leg.  Mark the locations of the U-bolts on each side of the aluminum angle, ensuring they are positioned at least 26 inches away from the tower leg bolts to provide adequate clearance for the mast and antenna (as discussed above). &#x20;

Use a bridge reamer to align and slightly enlarge the drilled holes as needed before installation. Secure each aluminum angle to the tower using bolts, along with washers, lock washers, and nuts. Then attach a vertical mast (1.5 inch / 16 gauge / 5 foot) to both ends of each aluminum angle. Each mast should be clamped to two pieces of aluminum angle using U-bolts sized for a 1.5-inch pipe, along with toothed pip brackets, washers, lock washers, and nuts. Position the masts so that there is approximately equal free length above and below the aluminum angles (about 1.5 ft on each end).  To ensure that the mast will be mounted vertically, make sure that the placement of the U-bolts on both lengths of aluminum angle are from the same distance from your center, or plumb line.  &#x20;

Finally, mount one antenna of each size to each mast to distribute wind load evenly. Place antennas of the same type or frequency on different vertical levels (top versus bottom) to minimize interference. Omnidirectional antennas should be installed at the top of one of the masts for optimal coverage.&#x20;

#### Tower taper considerations

Free standing towers taper inwards, so for mounts with a larger vertical span this will result in a difference of \~1" + of taper, and you will need to take that into consideration as your horizontal pole will be mounted on an angle inwards. This can be fixed by taking a secondary piece of angle on either the top or bottom mount (depending on if it is an inside or outside mount) and adjusting it by half of the difference between the top and bottom mounts. If the difference between the top and bottom mounting points is 1 inch, that means that the tower is tapering in on either side of the center line by 1/2 an inch.

Below, you can see the presence of an extra piece of angle attached to the top of the mount, moving the attachment point about a half of an inch inwards to account for the taper of the tower. This adjustment was done at the bottom to match the fact that it is tapering in at the top. (also note the double u-bolts to help negate potential twisting via wind load, as there is extra equipment mounted to the pole)

#### Mount and cable organization

It is important to always be aware of the climbing face, and to never obstruct tower access along the face. This includes avoiding mounting objects that would impede the horizontally welded ladder members of the tower. In the closeup picture above, it is mounted to the inside of the tower and is positioned pointing away from the climbing face. It is ok to mount on the inside of the climbing face, so long as it is positioned in such a way that it does not impede foot or handholds. &#x20;

Always practice proper cable management. Never exceed 3ft of unsecured vertical cable, or 1ft for horizontal. Never place cable where it could be stepped on, always secure to vertical or diagonal tower sections, and if necessary to the bottom of horizontal tower pieces. Keep in mind that towers can accumulate a lot of ice, which will eventually chip off and fall. Placing cables on the underside of horizontal surfaces helps mitigate potential damage by falling objects.&#x20;
